scenes.narration: Somewhere in the North Sea, a platform pumps oil from beneath the seabed. The money it earns ends up in one of the largest investment funds on Earth.
Norway's oil fund was worth about 2.1 trillion dollars at the end of September 2026. Divide that by every person in the country, and it comes to about 375,000 dollars each.

scenes.visual_objective: Camera-driven vector map: highlighted countries, animated routes with moving packets, flow arcs with particles, pulsing markers, callouts
scenes.narration: Through that fund, Norway owns on average 1.5 percent of every listed company in the world. 7,201 companies, in 68 countries.

keyframes.label: Average stake in world's listed companies

scenes.narration: Plenty of countries have found oil. Few have ended up like this. So what did Norway do differently? This is The Hidden Economics.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Before the oil, Norway lived from the sea and the mountains. Fishing boats worked the coast. By the nineteen-fifties its merchant fleet was described as the third largest in the world. And In 1905, Norsk Hydro began turning waterfalls into fertiliser.

scenes.visual_objective: Bars grow in a stagger with counting values
scenes.narration: It was a modest, hard-working economy, but not an especially rich one. In 1970, Norway's income per person was only about four-fifths of Sweden's, and behind Denmark's too.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Few believed there was oil under Norway's seabed at all. In 1958, the national geological survey told the government the chances could be discounted.

scenes.visual_objective: Camera-driven vector map: highlighted countries, animated routes with moving packets, flow arcs with particles, pulsing markers, callouts
scenes.narration: Still, Norway claimed its continental shelf. In 1965, it agreed a median line through the North Sea with Britain and Denmark, and handed out its first 22 production licences.

The first wells came up dry. Then, just before Christmas 1969, the American company Phillips Petroleum reported a find called Ekofisk. At the time, it was the largest offshore oil field ever discovered.
Oil started flowing from Ekofisk in June 1971. Norway had become an oil nation almost overnight.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Norway's first big decision was about control. In 1971, parliament adopted ten principles, later called the oil commandments, to keep the resource under national control and the industry serving the country.

In 1972, it created a state oil company, Statoil, and a regulator, the Petroleum Directorate. In 1985, the state also began holding direct stakes in oil fields itself. Today the government still owns 67 percent of Statoil's successor, Equinor.
The second decision was tax. Oil companies pay the normal 22 percent company tax, plus a special petroleum tax of 71.8 percent. Together, the state takes 78 percent of the profit at the margin.
So the oil pays the state three ways: taxes on company profits, its own share of the fields, and dividends from Equinor.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws
Bars grow in a stagger with counting values
scenes.narration: Those streams are enormous. In 2022, when energy prices spiked, the state's net cash flow from petroleum hit a record about 134 billion dollars. Even in a calmer year like last year, it was about 64 billion dollars.

scenes.visual_objective: Camera-driven vector map: highlighted countries, animated routes with moving packets, flow arcs with particles, pulsing markers, callouts
scenes.narration: Oil and gas made up 57 percent of the value of everything Norway exported in 2025. And through about 8,800 kilometres of pipelines, Norway's gas now covers more than 30 percent of all the gas used in the European Union and Britain.

keyframes.label: Oil & gas share of goods exports, 2025

scenes.narration: That much money arriving that fast is dangerous. Spend it all at home, and wages and prices surge, the currency soars, and every other industry struggles to compete. Economists call it the resource curse.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Norway's answer was to park the money abroad. In 1990, parliament created a petroleum fund. In May 1996, the first transfer, worth about 300 million dollars, went in.

Parliament sets the rules. The finance ministry owns the fund on the people's behalf. And the central bank's investment arm, created In 1998, manages it. One rule matters most: the fund is not allowed to invest in Norway at all.

scenes.visual_objective: Line chart draws progressively with the narration; event annotations pop on cues
scenes.narration: Then the money compounded. Here is the value of the fund at the end of each year, in billions of dollars. The line barely moves in the beginning, then it climbs, and climbs, past two thousand billion.
Here is the surprising part. According to the fund's manager, the oil money paid in accounts for less than half of its value today. The rest has been earned by the investments themselves.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws
Allocation arcs sweep one after another; legend counts in
scenes.narration: Most of the money, about 72 percent, is in shares. Around a quarter is in bonds. A small slice is in property and in renewable energy infrastructure.

scenes.visual_objective: Camera-driven vector map: highlighted countries, animated routes with moving packets, flow arcs with particles, pulsing markers, callouts
scenes.narration: And it is spread across the planet. The biggest share, 52.9 percent, is invested in the United States. Its largest single holdings are Nvidia, Apple and Alphabet.

Since it began buying shares, the fund has returned an average of 6.6 percent a year, or 4.3 percent after inflation and costs. But it is not a smooth ride: it lost minus 23 percent in the financial crisis, and minus 14 percent in 2022.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: The real secret is a rule about spending. Since 2001, the government may only take out, over time, what the fund is expected to earn after inflation. That was set at 4 percent, and cut to 3 percent in 2017.

In the budget for this year, the government planned to use about 56 billion dollars of oil money, about 2.8 percent of the fund. The IMF estimates that money from the fund now pays for about a quarter of all public spending.
Spending only the return means the capital is never used up. The oil is converted into shares, bonds and buildings around the world, and Norwegians who are not yet born will share in it too.

scenes.visual_objective: Line chart draws progressively with the narration; event annotations pop on cues
scenes.narration: It also protects the economy at home. Because spending is tied to the fund, not to this year's oil price, the IMF concluded that the rule and the fund would largely insulate Norway from a fall in oil revenue.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws
Allocation arcs sweep one after another; legend counts in
scenes.narration: Oil is still big, but it is not the whole story. In 2025, about four-fifths of Norway's output came from the mainland economy: the industries, services and public sector outside oil, gas and shipping.

That economy runs on an unusual model. About half of workers belong to a union. In wage talks, the industries that compete internationally negotiate first, and everyone else follows their lead, so pay keeps in step with what exporters can afford.

Income is spread evenly, and trust is high. In the latest OECD survey, 57 percent of Norwegians said they trusted their national government, against 40 percent across the OECD. Trust makes long-term rules, like the fund's, easier to keep.

But there is a warning sign. The OECD says Norway's productivity growth is now among the lowest in the OECD, and its lead in living standards over other rich countries has narrowed, from about 42% to 27% in fifteen years.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: The first risk is the oil price. After the summer of twenty fourteen, oil fell to around a third of its level. Norway's currency weakened by about 30 percent, and unemployment rose from 3.6 to 4.7 percent.

scenes.visual_objective: Bars grow in a stagger with counting values
scenes.narration: The second is time. More than half of Norway's known oil and gas, 57 percent, has already been produced. Output is forecast to fall by the end of the decade, as the world tries to move away from fossil fuels.

The third is age. Today there are about three people of working age for every Norwegian over sixty-five. By 2050, official projections imply about two. Pensions and care will cost more, just as oil money starts to shrink.
And the fund itself is exposed to the world's markets. In the manager's own stress test, a fragmented world economy could knock 37 percent off its value.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: So why is Norway so rich? Not just because it found oil. Because of what it decided to do next. It kept control of the resource. It taxed it heavily. It saved the money abroad, and it spends only the return.
The oil will run out one day. The rules are designed so that the fortune does not. In the IMF's words, Norway faces the future from a position of strength. This is The Hidden Economics.
